A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GMS-EB and GMS-DH research, despite the changed title and format. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v3 reports original routing experiments, including hypervolume and runtime comparisons, pruning ablations, training curves and zero-shot generalization results.

after.justification: v5 retains those original experiments and adds multigraph capacitated vehicle-routing results, additional neural comparisons and three-objective evaluations.

M1.justification: Section 4 and the matched architecture/training appendices retain the GREAT encoders, edge-based and dual-head decoders, preference conditioning, REINFORCE objectives and curriculum. The additional tasks and expanded implementation explanations do not establish a changed algorithm.

E1.justification: v5 adds MGMOCVRP on FLEX2/FIX2, combining capacity constraints with two conflicting total-distance objectives. It also adds tri-objective MOTSP and MGMOTSP across several distributions and instance sizes (Tables 11, 16–17). v3's multigraph experiments covered TSP-family problems, and all its evaluations were bi-objective.

E2.justification: v5 adds evaluated GREAT-based GRBM and GOAL-based GOBM comparators, including augmented variants, across retained routing tasks and MGMOCVRP (Table 6). It also introduces HGS for MGMOCVRP (Tables 1 and 11). The existing MBM, Euclidean CNH, evolutionary algorithms and relevant heuristics remain.

E3.justification: The existing bi-objective evaluation and training protocols are retained. Added tri-objective experiments use 105 heuristic subproblems and 105 or 1035 neural preferences, with three-dimensional hypervolume reference points (Tables 16–17; Appendix E). MGMOCVRP also receives task-specific reference points. These extend protocols for new experiments rather than revise the earlier evaluations.

E4.justification: The learned-versus-simple pruning and reward ablations, training analyses and zero-shot tests already appear in v3 and are retained. v5 extends the pre-pruning ablation to MGMOCVRP (Table 1) and compares 105 versus 1035 neural preferences on tri-objective tasks (Tables 16–17), adding evidence about pruning and inference-budget sensitivity.

E5.justification: Both versions average hypervolume over test instances and report runtimes. Neither reports repeated training-run counts, seeds, error bars, confidence intervals or statistical significance tests; the added results introduce no new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Matched earlier benchmark results retain their values and runtimes, but v5 adds substantial results for new tasks and comparators. For example, MGMOCVRP FLEX2-50 yields HV 0.89 for HGS and 0.86 for augmented GMS-EB (Table 1). Tri-objective XASY100 yields 0.64 for GMS-DH versus 0.68 for MBM with 105 preferences (Table 16). These are newly reported settings, not performance changes under v3's settings.

T1.justification: v5 explicitly requires the Chebyshev reference value to lie strictly below the minimum of each objective, whereas v3 only calls it an ideal value. New Appendix B.2 provides graph-size and decoding-complexity arguments for line-graph and virtual-node transformations. The Pareto definitions, scalarizations and Proposition 1 remain otherwise unchanged; its proof is still omitted.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the first neural multigraph-routing solvers, their two construction strategies and competitive performance with different scalability tradeoffs. v5's introduction additionally claims that naive extensions of existing single-objective asymmetric solvers perform poorly, extending v3's comparison of existing methods' supported inputs and tasks.

C2.justification: v5 adds explanations involving parallel-edge permutation invariance and graph transformations, and explains the existing omission of MatNet from large-instance evaluations. Appendix H.4 newly attributes the retained FIX10-100 weakness to the selection decoder's growing action space; H.5 qualifies objective-count scalability with the new GMS-DH XASY100 failure. Earlier training-cost and pruning-context limitations remain.

D1.justification: v5 replaces the promised future code release with a stated public implementation link. It also specifies uniform training-preference sampling, evenly spaced evaluation preferences, and construction details for GRBM/GOBM and the added tasks. Existing hardware, hyperparameters, curriculum and parameter counts remain documented as before. Repository contents were not independently verified.

R1.justification: Appendix A.2 and new Appendix B substantially expand research positioning, including POCCO, EFormer and hierarchical graph-partitioning work. v5 distinguishes encoding incompatibility from theoretically extendable edge-based methods and develops explicit novelty comparisons against prior AR/NAR combinations and dual-decoder systems. This goes beyond adding citations to the existing review.

P1.justification: The introduction is substantially rewritten around encoder and decoder incompatibilities, and multigraph-related discussion is consolidated into Section 2.2. A dedicated Extended Motivation appendix reorganizes the architectural rationale, graph-transformation alternatives and technical novelty. Experimental subsections and appendices are reorganized, although most method exposition is retained.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column conference formatting. Architecture diagrams are redrawn with example graphs and autoregressive loops, and a graph-transformation figure is added. Table 1 gains MGMOCVRP, new comparison/result tables appear, and v3's separate time-window tables are merged into v5 Table 12. Training plots are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: v3's broad applicability claims relied on TSP-family multigraph experiments and one general asymmetric neural baseline. v5 adds capacity-constrained multigraph routing, three-objective tests, two neural comparators and HGS, substantially strengthening tests of generality and comparative effectiveness (Tables 1, 6, 11, 16–17). The expanded architectural rationale and explicit failure cases also improve the argument's clarity and qualification. Evaluation remains synthetic and lacks statistical uncertainty, but these retained limitations do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.
